claim: Inherited retinal degenerations (IRDs) constitute a group of clinically and genetically diverse vision-impairing disorders.
source: Inherited retinal degenerations (IRDs) constitute a group of clinically and genetically diverse vision-impairing disorders.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about IRDs that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is the most common form of IRD.
source: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP), the most common form of IRD, is characterized by gradual dysfunction and degeneration of rod photoreceptors, followed by the loss of cone photoreceptors.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge and is consistent with the literature.

claim: RP is characterized by gradual dysfunction and degeneration of rod photoreceptors, followed by the loss of cone photoreceptors.
source: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP), the most common form of IRD, is characterized by gradual dysfunction and degeneration of rod photoreceptors, followed by the loss of cone photoreceptors.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of RP from scientific knowledge.

claim: Reserpine was identified as a lead molecule for maintaining rod survival in mouse and human retinal organoids as well as in the rd16 mouse.
source: Recently, we identified reserpine as a lead molecule for maintaining rod survival in mouse and human retinal organoids as well as in the rd16 mouse, which phenocopy Leber congenital amaurosis caused by mutations in the cilia-centrosomal gene CEP290 (Chen et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous publication by the authors.

claim: The rd16 mouse phenocopies Leber congenital amaurosis caused by mutations in the cilia-centrosomal gene CEP290.
source: Recently, we identified reserpine as a lead molecule for maintaining rod survival in mouse and human retinal organoids as well as in the rd16 mouse, which phenocopy Leber congenital amaurosis caused by mutations in the cilia-centrosomal gene CEP290 (Chen et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: At postnatal day (P) 68, when males and females are analyzed together, the reserpine-treated rats exhibit higher rod-derived scotopic b-wave amplitudes compared to the controls.
source: At postnatal day (P) 68, when males and females are analyzed together, the reserpine-treated rats exhibit higher rod-derived scotopic b-wave amplitudes compared to the controls with little or no change in scotopic a-wave or cone-derived photopic b-wave.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically ERG measurements.

claim: At P68, reserpine-treated rats show little or no change in scotopic a-wave or cone-derived photopic b-wave when males and females are analyzed together.
source: At postnatal day (P) 68, when males and females are analyzed together, the reserpine-treated rats exhibit higher rod-derived scotopic b-wave amplitudes compared to the controls with little or no change in scotopic a-wave or cone-derived photopic b-wave.
evidence: This is based on experimental ERG data from the study.

claim: Reserpine-treated female rats display enhanced scotopic a- and b-waves and photopic b-wave responses at P68.
source: Interestingly, the reserpine-treated female rats display enhanced scotopic a- and b-waves and photopic b-wave responses at P68, along with a better contrast threshold and increased outer nuclear layer thickness.
evidence: This is supported by experimental ERG data from female rats specifically.

claim: Reserpine-treated female rats show better contrast threshold at P68.
source: Interestingly, the reserpine-treated female rats display enhanced scotopic a- and b-waves and photopic b-wave responses at P68, along with a better contrast threshold and increased outer nuclear layer thickness.
evidence: This is based on optokinetic tracking measurements in the study.

claim: Reserpine-treated female rats show increased outer nuclear layer thickness at P68.
source: Interestingly, the reserpine-treated female rats display enhanced scotopic a- and b-waves and photopic b-wave responses at P68, along with a better contrast threshold and increased outer nuclear layer thickness.
evidence: This is supported by OCT and histological measurements in the study.

claim: Female rats demonstrate better preservation of both rod and cone photoreceptors following reserpine treatment.
source: The female rats demonstrate better preservation of both rod and cone photoreceptors following reserpine treatment.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing preserved photoreceptor structure.

claim: Retinal transcriptome analysis reveals sex-specific responses to reserpine.
source: Retinal transcriptome analysis reveals sex-specific responses to reserpine, with significant upregulation of phototransduction genes and proteostasis-related pathways, and notably, genes associated with stress response.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reserpine treatment results in significant upregulation of phototransduction genes.
source: Retinal transcriptome analysis reveals sex-specific responses to reserpine, with significant upregulation of phototransduction genes and proteostasis-related pathways, and notably, genes associated with stress response.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing increased expression of phototransduction genes.

claim: Reserpine treatment results in significant upregulation of proteostasis-related pathways.
source: Retinal transcriptome analysis reveals sex-specific responses to reserpine, with significant upregulation of phototransduction genes and proteostasis-related pathways, and notably, genes associated with stress response.
evidence: This is supported by pathway enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Reserpine treatment results in upregulation of genes associated with stress response.
source: Retinal transcriptome analysis reveals sex-specific responses to reserpine, with significant upregulation of phototransduction genes and proteostasis-related pathways, and notably, genes associated with stress response.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis from RNA-seq data.

claim: IRDs are caused by mutations in over 280 genes.
source: Inherited retinal degenerations (IRDs) are a diverse group of vision-deteriorating disorders caused by mutations in over 280 genes (Duncan et al., 2018; RetNet, https://retnet.org; August 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and the RetNet database.

claim: IRDs share a common outcome of gradual loss of photoreceptor cells.
source: Despite their genetic diversity, these disorders share a common outcome, which is the gradual loss of photoreceptor cells (Farrar et al., 2017; Swaroop et al., 2010; Wright et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA) is characterized by vision loss congenitally or during early infancy.
source: Among the more severe forms of IRDs is Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA), which is characterized by vision loss congenitally or during early infancy.
evidence: This is a well-established clinical characteristic of LCA from scientific knowledge.

claim: Retinal ciliopathy caused by mutations in CEP290 accounts for 20–25% of LCA.
source: The retinal ciliopathy caused by mutations in CEP290 accounts for 20–25% of LCA (Coppieters et al., 2010; Leroy et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) affects 1 in 3000–4000 individuals.
source: On the other hand, retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is the most common form of IRDs, affecting 1 in 3000–4000 individuals, and characterized by the primary degeneration of rod photoreceptors, followed by the loss of cone photoreceptors (Cross et al., 2022; Farrar et al., 2017; Verbakel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published epidemiological studies.

claim: The initial symptom of RP is reduced night vision, followed by gradual constriction of the visual field, often resulting in tunnel vision.
source: The initial symptom is reduced night vision, which is followed by a gradual constriction of the visual field, often resulting in tunnel vision.
evidence: This is a well-established clinical progression of RP from scientific knowledge.

claim: Mutations in the rhodopsin (RHO) gene are a major cause of retinal degeneration.
source: Mutations in the rhodopsin (RHO) gene, encoding the light-sensing visual pigment essential for phototransduction in rod photoreceptors, are a major cause of retinal degeneration (Athanasiou et al., 2018), with the P23H change accounting for over 10% of autosomal dominant RP (adRP) cases in the US (Sullivan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The P23H change in rhodopsin accounts for over 10% of autosomal dominant RP (adRP) cases in the US.
source: Mutations in the rhodopsin (RHO) gene, encoding the light-sensing visual pigment essential for phototransduction in rod photoreceptors, are a major cause of retinal degeneration (Athanasiou et al., 2018), with the P23H change accounting for over 10% of autosomal dominant RP (adRP) cases in the US (Sullivan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Visual function at the macula is relatively preserved until later stages of the disease in many IRDs.
source: Notably, visual function at the macula, the cone-dominant central region, is relatively preserved until later stages of the disease in many IRDs (Cideciyan and Jacobson, 2019; Cross et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The precise mechanisms through which mutations cause photoreceptor cell death in IRDs are not yet fully understood.
source: The precise mechanisms through which mutations cause photoreceptor cell death in IRDs are not yet fully understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Studies using animal models have shed light on several pathways involved in photoreceptor cell death in IRDs.
source: Nevertheless, studies using animal models have shed light on several pathways involved in photoreceptor cell death. These include abnormal photoreceptor outer segment morphogenesis, mitochondrial dysfunction, unfolded protein responses associated with the accumulation of misfolded protein in the endoplasmic reticulum, metabolic overload, aberrant protein trafficking, and chronic activation of phototransduction, among others (Bales and Gross, 2016; Chen et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022; Lobanova et al., 2013; Pierce, 2001; Power et al., 2020; Won et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: The only approved treatment for IRDs to date is a gene replacement therapy for one form of LCA caused by mutations in the gene RPE65.
source: To date, the only approved treatment is a gene replacement therapy for one form of LCA caused by mutations in the gene RPE65 (Russell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature about the approved therapy.

claim: Extensive genetic heterogeneity of IRDs poses a significant challenge for developing gene-specific therapies.
source: Extensive genetic heterogeneity of IRDs poses a significant challenge for developing gene-specific therapies, which in turn restricts the broad applicability of such interventions across a range of patient populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known genetic diversity of IRDs and the practical challenges of therapy development.

claim: Most IRD mutations are rare and often limited to a small number of patients or families.
source: Most IRD mutations are rare and often limited to a small number of patients or families; therefore, developing targeted interventions is less feasible due to the associated costs.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the genetic landscape of IRDs.

claim: Gene-agnostic therapies can reach larger patient cohorts than gene-specific therapies.
source: In contrast, gene-agnostic therapies can reach larger patient cohorts.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the nature of gene-agnostic versus gene-specific approaches.

claim: LaVail, Steinberg and colleagues were among the first to show therapeutic potential of many different neuroprotective factors in animal models of IRDs.
source: LaVail, Steinberg and colleagues were among the first to show therapeutic potential of many different neuroprotective factors in animal models of IRDs (LaVail et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a historical publication.

claim: Many different neurotrophic factors have been used in animal models and/or clinical trials with promising results.
source: Since then, many different neurotrophic factors, such as ciliary neurotrophic factor, rod-derived cone viability factor and pigment epithelium-derived factor, have been used in animal models and/or clinical trials with promising results (Byrne et al., 2015; Do Rhee et al., 2022; Michelis et al., 2021; Wen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Neuroprotection is predicted to slow down the rate of degeneration and preserve retinal function.
source: Neuroprotection including the use of antioxidant and anti-apoptotic compounds is predicted to slow down the rate of degeneration and preserve retinal function (Leinonen et al., 2024; Pinilla et al., 2022; Tolone et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and represents a hypothesis based on existing evidence.

claim: Photoreceptor cell death is the final outcome and the cause of vision loss in all IRDs.
source: Given that photoreceptor cell death is the final outcome and the cause of vision loss in all IRDs (Wright et al., 2010), we had proposed identification of therapeutic targets by examining the convergence of molecular pathways induced by divergent disease-causing IRD mutations (Swaroop et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Reserpine was identified through an unbiased large screen of small molecules based on survival of rod photoreceptors using retinal organoids derived from induced pluripotent stem cells of rd16 mice.
source: We recently reported an unbiased large screen of small molecules based on survival of rod photoreceptors using retinal organoids derived from induced pluripotent stem cells of rd16 mice (Chen et al., 2023), which phenocopies CEP290-LCA (Chang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous publication.

claim: Reserpine augmented rod survival in CEP290-LCA patient-derived retinal organoids and in the rd16 mouse retina in vivo.
source: Reserpine, the lead molecule identified by this screen, augmented rod survival in CEP290-LCA patient-derived retinal organoids and as well as in the rd16 mouse retina in vivo (Chen et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous publication.

claim: The neuroprotective effect of reserpine was achieved, at least in part, through the restoration of the balance between autophagy and the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: The neuroprotective effect of reserpine was achieved, at least in part, through the restoration of the balance between autophagy and the ubiquitin-proteasome system, the stress-response pathways maintaining cellular proteostasis (Chen et al., 2023; Villarejo-Zori et al., 2021; Weinberg et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature including the authors' previous work.

claim: The RHO P23H mutation reportedly causes protein misfolding and secondary proteasome defect leading to photoreceptor cell death.
source: In this study, we evaluated the therapeutic potential of reserpine for adRP caused by the RHO P23H mutation, which reportedly causes protein misfolding and secondary proteasome defect leading to photoreceptor cell death (Illing et al., 2002; Kaushal and Khorana, 1994; Qiu et al., 2019; Sakami et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Reserpine preserved photoreceptor cell survival and retinal function in the P23H-1 rat model.
source: We demonstrate that reserpine preserved photoreceptor cell survival and retinal function, with a more pronounced effect observed in female rats.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ERG, OCT, and histology presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reserpine has a more pronounced effect on photoreceptor preservation in female rats compared to male rats.
source: We demonstrate that reserpine preserved photoreceptor cell survival and retinal function, with a more pronounced effect observed in female rats.
evidence: This is supported by sex-specific analysis of experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The pathways modulated by reserpine were enriched in proteostasis-related processes.
source: Consistent with our previous study showing the efficacy of reserpine for CEP290-LCA IRD, the pathways modulated by reserpine were enriched in proteostasis-related processes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and pathway enrichment analysis in the manuscript.

claim: As early as P36, P23H-1 rats exhibited a reduction in the amplitude of scotopic a- and b-waves compared to wild-type animals.
source: As early as P36, P23H-1 rats exhibited a reduction in the amplitude of scotopic a- and b-waves compared to wild-type animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The decline in retinal function in P23H-1 rats continued progressively through P57.
source: The decline in retinal function continued progressively through P57, at which point the remaining function was comparable to that observed at P156.
evidence: This is based on ERG measurements at multiple time points.

claim: Studies on myopia using chicken eyes previously showed the effects of intravitreally injected reserpine could persist for more than 18 days after the injection.
source: Studies on myopia using chicken eyes previously showed the effects of intravitreally injected reserpine could persist for more than 18 days after the injection (Ohngemach et al., 1997; Schaeffel et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Intravitreally injected drug of similar molecular weight to reserpine could persist at concentration higher than 2 ng/mL throughout the entire observed period, up to 7 days in rat eye.
source: Our pharmacokinetic study in rat eye with another compound of similar molecular weight had shown that intravitreally injected drug could persist at concentration higher than 2 ng/mL throughout the entire observed period, up to 7 days (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on unpublished pharmacokinetic data from the authors.

claim: Two intravitreal injections of either vehicle or reserpine did not result in corneal or lens opacity, nor did they cause observable retinal inflammation in animals.
source: Two intravitreal injections of either vehicle or reserpine did not result in corneal or lens opacity, nor did they cause observable retinal inflammation in animals.
evidence: This is based on clinical observations during the study.

claim: The scotopic b-wave amplitude at P68 was 388.6±136.1 µV in reserpine-treated group and 277.8±62.4 µV in control group (p<0.05).
source: The amplitude was 388.6±136.1 µV in reserpine-treated group, while it was 277.8±62.4 µV in control group (p<0.05).
evidence: This is based on ERG measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: Most individuals with higher amplitude in scotopic b-wave at P68 were female rats in the reserpine-treated group.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, most individuals with higher amplitude in scotopic b-wave were female rats whereas no difference was evident in male and female rats in control group.
evidence: This is based on sex-specific analysis of ERG data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Female rats showed slower progression in decrease of scotopic b-wave response between P54 and P68.
source: Female rats also showed slower progression in decrease of scotopic b-wave response between P54 and P68 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on longitudinal ERG data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Retinal degeneration in P23H-1 rats does not progress synchronously throughout the retina, but dorsal retina is affected more severely.
source: Retinal degeneration in P23H-1 rats does not progress synchronously throughout the retina, but dorsal retina is affected more severely (García-Ayuso et al., 2013; LaVail et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: P23H mutations in RHO gene mainly affects rod photoreceptor cells that constitute more than 97.5% of photoreceptor cells in rat retina.
source: P23H mutations in RHO gene mainly affects rod photoreceptor cells that constitute more than 97.5% of photoreceptor cells in rat retina (Szél et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Treatment with reserpine preserved the ONL thickness of the dorsal retina at 1,000 μm distant from the optic nerve head in female rats.
source: Treatment with reserpine could preserve the ONL thickness of the dorsal retina at 1,000 μm distant from the optic nerve head, which was 17.93±0.96 μm compared to 15.29±0.73 μm in the control group.
evidence: This is based on OCT measurements with statistical comparison.

claim: The number of nuclei in the ONL in SD rats is 10–14.
source: The number of nuclei in the ONL in SD rats is 10–14 (García-Ayuso et al., 2013), but it was 3–4 nuclei in vehicle treated P23H-1 rats and 5–6 nuclei in reserpine-treated P23H-1 rats.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature and histological data from the current study.

claim: In P23H-1 rats, early changes such as increase in pyknotic nuclei can be detected as early as at P10 in the dorsal retina.
source: In P23H-1 rats, early changes such as increase in pyknotic nuclei can be detected as early as at P10 in the dorsal retina, which is followed by progressive loss of photoreceptor nuclei and shortening of rod inner and outer segments (LaVail et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In RP, cone photoreceptors gradually degenerate after rod photoreceptor loss.
source: In RP, cone photoreceptors gradually degenerate after rod photoreceptor loss (Campochiaro and Mir, 2018), and preserving cone photoreceptors can be particularly beneficial for patients in advanced stages of the disease.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The reserpine-treated female retina showed a higher number of cones at approximately 2000 μm dorsal to the optic nerve head.
source: When cone photoreceptors were counted every 500 μm across the retina, the reserpine-treated female retina showed a higher number of cones at approximately 2000 μm dorsal to the optic nerve head and relatively preserved cone morphology (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on cone arrestin immunostaining and counting shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) showed distinct clustering of WT and P23H transcriptomes.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) showed distinct clustering of WT and P23H transcriptomes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on PCA analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Female and male retinas separated within WT as well as treated and untreated groups in PCA analysis.
source: Interestingly, female and male retinas separated within WT as well as treated and untreated groups, suggesting a notable influence of biological sex.
evidence: This is based on PCA analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Combined analyses of both male and female WT and P23H retinas revealed 652 genes differentially expressed at significance threshold of adjusted p-value <0.05 and absolute fold change >2.
source: Combined analyses of both male and female WT and P23H retinas revealed 652 genes differentially expressed at significance threshold of adjusted p-value <0.05 and absolute fold change >2 (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Phototransduction was observed to be strongly downregulated in P23H retinas.
source: Phototransduction was observed to be strongly downregulated in P23H retinas with several genes showing marked sex-specific trends in the mutant (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is based on gene set enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figures 5D and E.

claim: Many housekeeping and inflammation related gene sets were significantly impacted by P23H-linked transcriptomic changes.
source: Many housekeeping and inflammation related gene sets were significantly impacted by P23H-linked transcriptomic changes.
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Many of the pathways enriched in this study were also enriched in two published transcriptome datasets from P23H and WT rodent models.
source: We analyzed two published transcriptome datasets from P23H and WT rodent models to evaluate our observations and identified that many of the pathways were enriched in those studies (Leinonen et al., 2020; Vats et al., 2022; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis with published datasets shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pathways relating to transcription, translation and cellular transport were markedly altered in P23H mutant retinas.
source: Among the prominent pathways, those relating to transcription, translation and cellular transport that deal with production, quality control and transport of biomolecules were markedly altered in P23H mutant retinas (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The female P23H rat retina revealed 548 over-expressed genes whereas 796 genes showed lower expression compared to WT.
source: The female P23H rat retina revealed 548 over-expressed genes whereas 796 genes showed lower expression.
evidence: This is based on sex-specific differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Male retinas demonstrated stronger differential trends with 2542 and 1580 over- and under-expressing genes, respectively, compared to WT.
source: Male retinas demonstrated stronger differential trends with 2542 and 1580 over- and under-expressing genes, respectively.
evidence: This is based on sex-specific differential gene expression analysis.

claim: In female retinas, the reserpine treatment resulted in higher expression of 1437 genes, whereas 352 genes showed lower expression.
source: In female retinas, the reserpine treatment resulted in higher expression of 1437 genes, whereas 352 genes showed lower expression (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis of reserpine-treated versus untreated female retinas.

claim: Expression profiles of differential genes in reserpine-treated female retinas clustered closer to WT than untreated mutant retinas.
source: Expression profiles of differential genes clustered closer to WT than untreated mutant retinas as evidence by the dendrogram in the heatmap of Figure 6A.
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Male P23H retinas showed only 180 over and 580 under expressing genes in response to reserpine.
source: In contrast, male P23H retinas showed only 180 over and 580 under expressing genes, however, unlike female samples, male differential genes did not cluster with WT suggesting a distinct reserpine response in the two sexes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis of reserpine-treated versus untreated male retinas.

claim: Elevated expression across phototransduction genes was observed in treated female retinas, including that of the gene coding for rhodopsin.
source: Most promisingly, we observed elevated expression across phototransduction genes in treated female retinas, including that of the gene coding for rhodopsin (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Key rod photoreceptor transcription factors - NRL, NR2E3, and CRX - responded to reserpine treatment.
source: Also responding to reserpine were the key rod photoreceptor transcription factors - NRL, NR2E3, and CRX (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: MEF2C showed an opposite trend of lower expression in reserpine-treated female retinas.
source: Interestingly, MEF2C, another transcription factor associated with rod gene expression (Hao et al., 2011) showed an opposite trend of lower expression in reserpine-treated female retinas (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Proteostasis linked pathways such as proteasome, endocytosis, lysosome and ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis showed notable drug response.
source: Notable drug response was observed in proteostasis linked pathways such as proteasome, endocytosis, lysosome and ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis, which had at least five significantly over-expressing genes and a minimum 5% of the pathways impacted (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Signaling pathways such as p53, TGF-beta and hippo were impacted by reserpine linked over-expression.
source: Furthermore, signaling pathways such as p53, TGF-beta and hippo were also impacted by reserpine linked over-expression.
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: P62 (Sqstm1) showed robust overexpression in reserpine-treated female retinas.
source: To further understand upregulation of proteostasis network, we checked two key factors p62 (Sqstm1) and Nrf2 (Nfe2l2) and identified robust overexpression in the former while the latter did not show significant response despite an increasing trend (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Nrf2 (Nfe2l2) did not show significant response to reserpine despite an increasing trend.
source: To further understand upregulation of proteostasis network, we checked two key factors p62 (Sqstm1) and Nrf2 (Nfe2l2) and identified robust overexpression in the former while the latter did not show significant response despite an increasing trend (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The gene coding for Akt1 was significantly responsive to reserpine.
source: Similarly, the gene coding for Akt1, a prominent pro-survival serine/threonine kinase and a member of the p53 network, was significantly responsive to reserpine, as were other genes of the pathway (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: KEGG neuronal system genesets including multiple synapse related processes showed higher gene expression in female P23H retinas upon reserpine treatment.
source: Finally, KEGG neuronal system genesets including multiple synapse related processes were observed to show higher gene expression in female P23H retinas upon reserpine treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Reserpine-treated P23H retina exhibits improved visual function with higher and consistent potency in female rats.
source: Reserpine-treated P23H retina exhibits improved visual function, with higher and consistent potency in female rats, where scotopic a- and b-wave and photopic b-wave are better preserved.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the ERG data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Structural analysis with OCT and histology reveals prominent response in dorsal regions of reserpine-treated retina where degeneration is known to be severe and linked with light exposure.
source: Structural analysis with OCT and histology also reveals prominent response in dorsal regions of reserpine-treated retina where degeneration is known to be severe and linked with light exposure (Bogéa et al., 2015; García-Ayuso et al., 2013; LaVail et al., 2018; Tam et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on OCT and histological data with citations to published literature about regional degeneration patterns.

claim: The photoreceptor response in P23H rat model was measured three weeks after the last reserpine injection, showing the longer-term effect of the treatment.
source: Notably, the photoreceptor response in P23H rat model was measured three weeks after the last reserpine injection, showing the longer-term effect of the treatment.
evidence: This is based on the experimental timeline and measurements in the study.

claim: Some of the drug-responding pathways are reportedly dysregulated in another retinal degeneration model.
source: Remarkably, some of the drug-responding pathways are reportedly dysregulated in another retinal degeneration model (Jiang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Reserpine was originally FDA-approved for hypertension treatment.
source: Reserpine, originally FDA-approved for hypertension treatment, inhibits vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT), depleting catecholamines by preventing their storage and leading to their metabolism by monoamine oxidase (Koch et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature and is established knowledge about reserpine.

claim: Reserpine inhibits vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT), depleting catecholamines by preventing their storage and leading to their metabolism by monoamine oxidase.
source: Reserpine, originally FDA-approved for hypertension treatment, inhibits vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT), depleting catecholamines by preventing their storage and leading to their metabolism by monoamine oxidase (Koch et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature and is established knowledge about reserpine's mechanism.

claim: Intravitreal reserpine injections in chickens depleted retinal dopamine and serotonin, with effects lasting up to 21 days.
source: Intravitreal reserpine injections in chickens depleted retinal dopamine and serotonin, with effects lasting up to 21 days (Ohngemach et al., 1997; Schaeffel et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: ERG measurements and spectral sensitivity showed no differences in normal retinas treated with reserpine.
source: However, ERG measurements and spectral sensitivity showed no differences in normal retinas treated with reserpine (Schaeffel et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Rodent photoreceptors express D2-like receptors and 5-HT3A receptors.
source: Rodent photoreceptors express D2-like receptors (Derouiche and Asan, 1999; Patel et al., 2003; Tran and Dickman, 1992) and 5-HT3A receptors (Masson, 2019), with D2-like receptor antagonists reducing rod response amplitude and kinetics, whereas agonists enhance the response (Jin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: D2-like receptor antagonists reduce rod response amplitude and kinetics, whereas agonists enhance the response.
source: Rodent photoreceptors express D2-like receptors (Derouiche and Asan, 1999; Patel et al., 2003; Tran and Dickman, 1992) and 5-HT3A receptors (Masson, 2019), with D2-like receptor antagonists reducing rod response amplitude and kinetics, whereas agonists enhance the response (Jin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Reserpine-induced catecholamine depletion likely reduces the scotopic b-wave amplitude at P54.
source: Reserpine-induced catecholamine depletion likely reduces the scotopic b-wave amplitude at P54 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A); however, no further decrease is detected after that, unlike a progressive reduction in untreated controls.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known mechanism of reserpine and the observed ERG data.

claim: Antagonists for D1-, D2-like or 5-HT2A receptors, as well as dopamine depletion, have shown protective effects in retinal disease models.
source: Antagonists for D1-, D2-like or 5-HT2A receptors, as well as dopamine depletion, have shown protective effects (Ogilvie and Speck, 2002; Tullis et al., 2015), and agonists for D2-like or 5-HT1A receptors have also demonstrated protective effects in different contexts (Collier et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Agonists for D2-like or 5-HT1A receptors have demonstrated protective effects in different contexts.
source: Antagonists for D1-, D2-like or 5-HT2A receptors, as well as dopamine depletion, have shown protective effects (Ogilvie and Speck, 2002; Tullis et al., 2015), and agonists for D2-like or 5-HT1A receptors have also demonstrated protective effects in different contexts (Collier et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Combination therapies targeting adrenergic, dopamine, and serotonin receptors appear to show promise for retinal protection in diabetic retinopathy and inherited retinal degeneration.
source: Combination therapies targeting adrenergic, dopamine, and serotonin receptors appear to show promise for retinal protection in diabetic retinopathy and inherited retinal degeneration (Kern et al., 2021; Leinonen et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Female and male P23H rats exhibit distinct sex-bias in disease profiles as well as response to reserpine.
source: Our study highlights a distinct sex-bias in disease profiles as well as response to reserpine in female and male P23H rats, where female rats exhibit significant recovery of retinal function as measured by ERG.
evidence: This is based on sex-specific analysis of ERG and transcriptomic data in the manuscript.

claim: Transcriptomic comparisons among WT, P23H mutant, and reserpine-treated mutant retinas showed distinct trends in female and male rats.
source: Transcriptomic comparisons among WT, P23H mutant, and reserpine-treated mutant retinas also showed distinct trends in female and male rats.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Though retinal transcriptomes from P23H retinas from both sexes deviate significantly from WT, many disease-linked enriched pathways are unique to a sex group.
source: Though retinal transcriptomes from P23H retinas from both sexes deviate significantly from WT, many disease-linked enriched pathways are unique to a sex group.
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis of sex-specific RNA-seq data.

claim: Retinal organoids derived from female LCA10 patients are more responsive to reserpine, while male-derived organoids show less consistent responses.
source: Our previous study demonstrated that retinal organoids derived from female LCA10 patients are more responsive to reserpine, while male-derived organoids show less consistent responses (Chen et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous publication.

claim: When striatal dopamine storage was impaired by the inhibition of VMAT by reserpine, a greater degree of dopamine deficits was observed in female mice.
source: When striatal dopamine storage was impaired by the inhibition of VMAT by reserpine, a greater degree of dopamine deficits was observed in female mice, suggesting that females possess a greater dopamine storage capacity (Ji et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: The greater depletions of striatal dopamine content in female mice was not estrogen dependent.
source: The greater depletions of striatal dopamine content in female mice was not estrogen dependent (Dluzen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Female rats were resistant to cognitive and motor deficits in reserpine-induced Parkinson's disease model.
source: Despite the increased responsiveness of dopamine levels in females, another study showed that female rats were resistant to cognitive and motor deficits in reserpine-induced Parkinson's disease model (Lima et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Some sex differences in response to reserpine are strain-dependent.
source: In contrast, Rivera-Garcia et al. suggested that some sex differences are strain-dependent, showing no significant difference in reserpine-evoked dopamine release between female and male Long-Evans rats, but observing sex differences in electrically stimulated dopamine release in Sprague-Dawley rats (Rivera-Garcia et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: 18-month-old female rats showed ERG changes according to menopausal status.
source: For instance, 18-month-old female rats showed ERG changes according to menopausal status, whereas no significant differences in ERG or retinal histology were observed between male and female rats at any other age (Chaychi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: The molecular target of reserpine in the retina remains unknown.
source: However, the molecular target of reserpine in the retina remains unknown although we note possibilities of a different associate in the retina.
evidence: This is a statement about the current limitation of knowledge from the study.

claim: Reasons for biological sex bias in drug response must be investigated with a focus on determining whether female and male retinas are predisposed differently to retinal pathology and interventions.
source: Additionally, reasons for biological sex bias in drug response must be investigated with a focus on determining whether female and male retinas are predisposed differently to retinal pathology and interventions.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions based on the findings.

claim: Hemizygous P23H-1 rats carry a single P23H transgene allele with a transgene copy number of 9, in addition to the normal two wild-type opsin alleles.
source: The hemizygous P23H-1 rats carry a single P23H transgene allele with a transgene copy number of 9, in addition to the normal two wild-type opsin alleles (Orhan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature describing the animal model.

claim: The ratio of transgene to endogenous opsin mRNA in hemizygous P23H-1 rats was 0.1:1.
source: The ratio of transgene to endogenous opsin mRNA was 0.1:1 (LaVail et al., 2018; Machida et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A total of 10,726 genes were captured across 19 samples after standard quality check and filtering in the RNA-seq analysis.
source: After standard quality check and filtering, a total of 10,726 genes were captured across 19 samples.
evidence: This is based on the RNA-seq data processing described in the methods.
